On a two-color partition series and its companionsThanks: First author partially supported by Simons Foundation Grant 633284

George E. Andrews and Mohamed El Bachraoui Address: The Pennsylvania State University, University Park, Pennsylvania 16802 Email address: andrews@math.psu.edu Address: Department of Mathematical Sciences, United Arab Emirates University, PO Box 15551, Al-Ain, UAE Email address: melbachraoui@uaeu.ac.ae
Date: August 24, 2026
Abstract.

We study the two-color distinct-part series S1​(q)S_{1}(q), equivalently Andrews’ generating function vd​(q)v_{d}(q) for strictly concave compositions, and its odd and even companions To​(q)T_{o}(q) and Te​(q)T_{e}(q). We determine the coefficients of S1​(q)S_{1}(q) modulo 44 and obtain a complete criterion for the resulting Ramanujan-type progressions. For the even companion, we give a direct overpartition interpretation of its coefficients and show that two natural partition families are each counted by half of those coefficients. For the eta-normalized odd companion C⁡(q)=(q,q)∞​To​(q)C(q)=(q;q)_{\infty}T_{o}(q), we prove a quintic self-similarity, derive exact vanishing relations and infinite sign changes for its coefficients, and show that c⁡(n)c(n) can be nonzero only when 24​n+2824n+28 is represented by x2+3​y2x^{2}+3y^{2}.

Key words and phrases: 
integer partitions, two-color partitions, concave compositions, false theta functions, qq-series, arithmetic progressions
2020 Mathematics Subject Classification
11P81, 11P83, 05A17, 33D15

1. Introduction and main results

Throughout we use the standard qq-shifted factorial notation; see, for example [12, Chapter 1]. Thus

(a,q)0=1,(a,q)n=∏j=0n−1(1−a​qj),(a,q)∞=∏j=0∞(1−a​qj),(a;q)_{0}=1,\qquad(a;q)_{n}=\prod_{j=0}^{n-1}(1-aq^{j}),\qquad(a;q)_{\infty}=\prod_{j=0}^{\infty}(1-aq^{j}),

and

(a1,…,ar;q)n=(a1;q)n⋯(ar;q)n,(a1,…,ar;q)∞=(a1;q)∞⋯(ar;q)∞.(a_{1},\dots,a_{r};q)_{n}=(a_{1};q)_{n}\cdots(a_{r};q)_{n},\qquad(a_{1},\dots,a_{r};q)_{\infty}=(a_{1};q)_{\infty}\cdots(a_{r};q)_{\infty}.

Integer partitions in which each part may occur in two colors (red and blue) have been studied extensively in recent years. For references on two-color partitions closely related to the present work, see, for instance, [2, 3, 5, 6, 8, 9, 10].

In this paper, the main series is

S1​(q):=∑n≥0qn​(−qn+1,q)∞2.S_{1}(q):=\sum_{n\geq 0}q^{n}\,(-q^{n+1};q)_{\infty}^{2}.

Thus S1​(q)S_{1}(q) is the generating function for the number of two-color partitions into distinct parts whose smallest part occurs in one prescribed color only, while every larger part may occur in either color or in both colors. The constant term counts the empty partition. The same series also appears in Andrews’ work on concave and convex compositions [4]. Indeed, if Vd​(n)V_{d}(n) denotes the number of strictly concave compositions of nn in the notation of [4], and

vd​(q):=∑n≥0Vd​(n)​qn,v_{d}(q):=\sum_{n\geq 0}V_{d}(n)q^{n},

then

vd​(q)=S1​(q).v_{d}(q)=S_{1}(q).

Here the central part contributes qnq^{n}, and the two strict sides independently select distinct parts greater than nn. Thus the congruence results for s1​(n)s_{1}(n) below may also be read as congruence results for strictly concave compositions. We record a simple companion identity.

Remark 1.

If both colors are required to occur in the smallest part, then the natural generating function is

S2​(q):=∑n≥1q2​n​(−qn+1,q)∞2.S_{2}(q):=\sum_{n\geq 1}q^{2n}\,(-q^{n+1};q)_{\infty}^{2}.

A short calculation gives

S2​(q)=3​(−q,q)∞2−1−2​S1​(q),S_{2}(q)=3(-q;q)_{\infty}^{2}-1-2S_{1}(q),

so this variant produces no essentially new series.

Writing

S1​(q)=∑n≥0s1​(n)​qn,S_{1}(q)=\sum_{n\geq 0}s_{1}(n)q^{n},

our first main result is the following complete description modulo 44 for the sequence {s1​(n)}\{s_{1}(n)\}.

Theorem 1.

For every n≥0n\geq 0,

s1​(n)≡{(−1)r(mod4),if ​n=r⁡(r+1)2​ for some ​r≥0,0(mod4),otherwise.s_{1}(n)\equiv\begin{cases}(-1)^{r}\pmod{4},&\text{if }n=\dfrac{r(r+1)}{2}\text{ for some }r\geq 0,\\ 0\pmod{4},&\text{otherwise.}\end{cases}

In particular, s1​(n)s_{1}(n) is odd if and only if nn is triangular.

Remark 2.

The parity assertion in Theorem 1 is also an immediate consequence of Andrews’ formula for vd​(q)v_{d}(q) in [4, Theorem 1, (1.4)]. In our notation that formula reads

S1​(q)=−Θ⁡(q)+2​(−q,q)∞2​∑n≥0qn⁡(3​n+1)/2​(1−q2​n+1),S_{1}(q)=-\Theta(q)+2(-q;q)_{\infty}^{2}\sum_{n\geq 0}q^{n(3n+1)/2}(1-q^{2n+1}),

where

Θ⁡(q)=∑r≥0(−1)r​qr⁡(r+1)/2.\Theta(q)=\sum_{r\geq 0}(-1)^{r}q^{r(r+1)/2}.

Reducing modulo 22 gives S1​(q)≡Θ⁡(q)(mod2)S_{1}(q)\equiv\Theta(q)\pmod{2}, and hence s1​(n)s_{1}(n) is odd exactly when nn is triangular. Theorem 1 refines this parity statement to a modulo 44 evaluation.

Since A​n+B=r⁡(r+1)2An+B=\frac{r(r+1)}{2} if and only if 8​A​n+8​B+1=(2​r+1)28An+8B+1=(2r+1)^{2}, Theorem 1 yields the next criterion.

Corollary 1.

Let A≥1A\geq 1 and 0≤B<A0\leq B<A. Then

s1​(A​n+B)≡0(mod4)(n≥0)s_{1}(An+B)\equiv 0\pmod{4}\qquad(n\geq 0)

if and only if 8​B+18B+1 is not a square modulo 8​A8A.

For odd primes pp, the congruence 8​B+1≡1(mod8)8B+1\equiv 1\pmod{8} shows that the square condition modulo 8​p8p is equivalent to the Legendre-symbol condition modulo pp.

Corollary 2.

Let pp be an odd prime. Then

s1​(p​n+B)≡0(mod4)(n≥0)s_{1}(pn+B)\equiv 0\pmod{4}\qquad(n\geq 0)

if and only if

(8​B+1p)=−1.\left(\frac{8B+1}{p}\right)=-1.

Hence for each odd prime pp there are exactly (p−1)/2(p-1)/2 such progressions modulo pp.

For example, Corollary 2 gives

s1​(3​n+2)≡0(mod4),s1​(5​n+2)≡s1​(5​n+4)≡0(mod4),s_{1}(3n+2)\equiv 0\pmod{4},\qquad s_{1}(5n+2)\equiv s_{1}(5n+4)\equiv 0\pmod{4},

and

s1​(7​n+2)≡s1​(7​n+4)≡s1​(7​n+5)≡0(mod4).s_{1}(7n+2)\equiv s_{1}(7n+4)\equiv s_{1}(7n+5)\equiv 0\pmod{4}.

The odd and even companion series are

To​(q):=∑m≥0q2​m​(−q,q)2​m(q,q2)m+1,Te​(q):=∑m≥0(−1,q)2​m​q2​m(q2,q2)m.T_{o}(q):=\sum_{m\geq 0}q^{2m}\frac{(-q;q)_{2m}}{(q;q^{2})_{m+1}},\qquad T_{e}(q):=\sum_{m\geq 0}\frac{(-1;q)_{2m}q^{2m}}{(q^{2};q^{2})_{m}}.

They arise naturally from the odd-even decomposition underlying our formulas for S1​(q)S_{1}(q); see Proposition 1 below.

An important series in this paper is the eta-normalized series C⁡(q)C(q) defined by

C⁡(q)=(q,q)∞​To​(q).C(q)=(q;q)_{\infty}T_{o}(q). (1.1)

Writing

C⁡(q)=∑n≥0c⁡(n)​qn,C(q)=\sum_{n\geq 0}c(n)q^{n},

the following main result shows that the sequence {c⁡(n)}\{c(n)\} has rich arithmetic properties.

Theorem 2.

For all n≥0n\geq 0,

c⁡(25​n+8)=c⁡(25​n+13)=c⁡(25​n+18)=c⁡(25​n+23)=0,c(25n+8)=c(25n+13)=c(25n+18)=c(25n+23)=0,

and

c⁡(25​n+28)=−c⁡(n).c(25n+28)=-c(n).

In particular, c⁡(n)c(n) changes sign infinitely often and assumes both positive and negative values infinitely often.

Iterating the relation c⁡(25​n+28)=−c⁡(n)c(25n+28)=-c(n) therefore produces infinite towers of coefficients with alternating signs.

The next result shows that the support of C⁡(q)C(q) is constrained by the binary quadratic form x2+3​y2x^{2}+3y^{2}, and its corollary gives exact vanishing progressions modulo p2p^{2} for every prime p≡2(mod3)p\equiv 2\pmod{3}.

Theorem 3.

If c⁡(n)≠0c(n)\neq 0, then

24​n+28=x2+3​y224n+28=x^{2}+3y^{2}

for some integers xx and yy. Consequently, if p≡2(mod3)p\equiv 2\pmod{3} is an odd prime and pp divides 6​n+76n+7 to odd order, then

c⁡(n)=0.c(n)=0.
Corollary 3.

Let p≡2(mod3)p\equiv 2\pmod{3} be an odd prime. Let rpr_{p} be the unique residue class modulo pp satisfying

6​rp+7≡0(modp).6r_{p}+7\equiv 0\pmod{p}.

Among the pp lifts of rpr_{p} modulo p2p^{2}, exactly one residue class satisfies

6​r+7≡0(modp2).6r+7\equiv 0\pmod{p^{2}}.

For each of the remaining p−1p-1 lifts rr, we have

c⁡(p2​n+r)=0(n≥0).c(p^{2}n+r)=0\qquad(n\geq 0).

For p=5p=5, Corollary 3 yields the four vanishing progressions in Theorem 2. For p=11p=11, it gives

c⁡(121​n+r)=0(n≥0),c(121n+r)=0\qquad(n\geq 0),

for

r∈{8,30,41,52,63,74,85,96,107,118}.r\in\{8,30,41,52,63,74,85,96,107,118\}.

The remainder of the paper will be organized as follows. The partition-theoretic results for the even companion and the comparison with OEIS A344650 are collected in Section 3. The analytic formulas for the companion series are collected in Section 4. The proofs are given in Sections 5–10, and the paper closes in Section 11 with final remarks, problems, and conjectures.

2. qq-Series Background

In this section we collect several well-known facts from the theory of basic hypergeometric series that will be needed in our proofs. We start with the qq-binomial theorem [1, Eq. (2.2.1)]

∑n≥0(a,q)n​zn(q,q)n=(a​z,q)∞(z,q)∞,\sum_{n\geq 0}\frac{(a;q)_{n}z^{n}}{(q;q)_{n}}=\frac{(az;q)_{\infty}}{(z;q)_{\infty}}, (2.1)

Euler’s identity [1, Eq. (1.2.5)]

(−q,q)∞=1(q,q2)∞,(-q;q)_{\infty}=\frac{1}{(q;q^{2})_{\infty}}, (2.2)

Euler’s expansion [1, Eq. (2.2.6)]

(z,q)∞=∑n≥0(−1)n​qn⁡(n−1)/2​zn(q,q)n,(z;q)_{\infty}=\sum_{n\geq 0}\frac{(-1)^{n}q^{n(n-1)/2}z^{n}}{(q;q)_{n}}, (2.3)

and Gauss’ sum [1, Eq. (2.2.13)]

(q2,q2)∞(q,q2)∞=∑n≥0qn⁡(n+1)/2.\frac{(q^{2};q^{2})_{\infty}}{(q;q^{2})_{\infty}}=\sum_{n\geq 0}q^{n(n+1)/2}. (2.4)

We need the following false theta evaluation [7, Eq. (9.4.14)]

∑n≥0(−q)n(−q2,q2)n=∑n≥0qn⁡(3​n+1)/2​(1−q2​n+1)\sum_{n\geq 0}\frac{(-q)^{n}}{(-q^{2};q^{2})_{n}}=\sum_{n\geq 0}q^{n(3n+1)/2}(1-q^{2n+1}) (2.5)

and Euler’s pentagonal theorem [1, Eq. (1.3.1)]

(q,q)∞=∑n≥0(−1)n​qn⁡(3​n+1)/2​(1−q2​n+1).(q;q)_{\infty}=\sum_{n\geq 0}(-1)^{n}q^{n(3n+1)/2}(1-q^{2n+1}). (2.6)

In addition, we will need Jacobi’s triple product [1, Eq. (2.2.10)]

∑n=−∞∞znqn2=(−zq,−q/z,q2;q2)∞\sum_{n=-\infty}^{\infty}z^{n}q^{n^{2}}=(-zq,-q/z,q^{2};q^{2})_{\infty} (2.7)

Finally, recall the definition of the basic hypergeometric series [12, Eq. (1.2.22)]:

ϕrr+1​[.a1;a2;…;ar+1b1;b2;…;br.;q;z]=∑n=0∞(a1;q)n(a2;q)n⋯(ar+1;q)n(q;q)n(b1;q)n⋯(br;q)n​zn.{}_{\,r+1\,}\phi_{\,r\,}\biggl[\genfrac{.}{.}{0.0pt}{}{a_1, a_2, \dots, a_{r+1}}{b_1, b_2, \dots, b_r};q;z\biggr]=\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}\frac{(a_{1};q)_{n}(a_{2};q)_{n}\cdots(a_{r+1};q)_{n}}{(q;q)_{n}(b_{1};q)_{n}\cdots(b_{r};q)_{n}}\,z^{n}.

Heine’s first transformation [12, (III.1)] states that

ϕ12​(a,bc,q,z)=(b,a​z,q)∞(c,z,q)∞​ϕ12​(c/b,za​z,q,b).{}_{2}\phi_{1}\!\left(\begin{matrix}a,b\\ c\end{matrix};q,z\right)=\frac{(b,az;q)_{\infty}}{(c,z;q)_{\infty}}{}_{2}\phi_{1}\!\left(\begin{matrix}c/b,z\\ az\end{matrix};q,b\right). (2.8)

3. Partition identities and strict odd-length partitions

The coefficients of the even companion admit a direct overpartition interpretation. Recall that an overpartition is a partition in which the first occurrence of a part may be overlined; see Corteel and Lovejoy [11]. Write

Te​(q)=1+∑N≥1te​(N)​qN.T_{e}(q)=1+\sum_{N\geq 1}t_{e}(N)q^{N}.

For m≥1m\geq 1, the mmth summand in the defining series for Te​(q)T_{e}(q) can be written as

2​q2​m1−q2​m​∏j=1m−11+q2​j1−q2​j​∏j=1m(1+q2​j−1).2\frac{q^{2m}}{1-q^{2m}}\prod_{j=1}^{m-1}\frac{1+q^{2j}}{1-q^{2j}}\prod_{j=1}^{m}(1+q^{2j-1}).

Thus, for N≥1N\geq 1, the coefficient te​(N)t_{e}(N) counts overpartitions of NN such that the largest part is even, only even parts may be overlined, and the odd parts are distinct; the factor 2​q2​m/(1−q2​m)2q^{2m}/(1-q^{2m}) records the two choices for the overline status of the largest part 2​m2m. In particular, te​(N)t_{e}(N) is even for every N≥1N\geq 1.

Definition 1.

For N≥1N\geq 1, let ae​(N)a_{e}(N) denote the number of ordinary partitions of NN whose first missing part among the positive integers not congruent to 1(mod4)1\pmod{4} is congruent to 3(mod4)3\pmod{4}. Equivalently, among the candidate parts

2,3,4,6,7,8,10,11,12,…,2,3,4,6,7,8,10,11,12,\dots,

the smallest candidate that does not occur is of the form 4​m+34m+3.

For N≥1N\geq 1, let be​(N)b_{e}(N) denote the number of overpartitions of NN such that the largest part is even and not overlined, only even parts may be overlined, and the odd parts are distinct.

The direct interpretation of te​(N)t_{e}(N) above shows immediately that

te​(N)=2​be​(N)(N≥1).t_{e}(N)=2b_{e}(N)\qquad(N\geq 1). (3.1)
Remark 3.

For N=6N=6, the eight overpartitions counted by te​(6)t_{e}(6) are

(6),(6¯),(4,2),(4¯,2),(4,2¯),(4¯,2¯),(2,2,2),(2¯,2,2).(6),\qquad(\overline{6}),\qquad(4,2),\qquad(\overline{4},2),\qquad(4,\overline{2}),\qquad(\overline{4},\overline{2}),\qquad(2,2,2),\qquad(\overline{2},2,2).

Thus te​(6)=8t_{e}(6)=8.

Restricting to the overpartitions with nonoverlined largest part leaves the four objects counted by be​(6)b_{e}(6):

(6),(4,2),(4,2¯),(2,2,2).(6),\qquad(4,2),\qquad(4,\overline{2}),\qquad(2,2,2).

Hence be​(6)=4b_{e}(6)=4.

The ordinary partitions counted by ae​(6)a_{e}(6) are

(4,2),(2,2,2),(2,2,1,1),(2,1,1,1,1).(4,2),\qquad(2,2,2),\qquad(2,2,1,1),\qquad(2,1,1,1,1).

In each case the relevant candidate parts begin

2,3,4,6,7,8,…,2,3,4,6,7,8,\dots,

and the first missing candidate is 33. Thus ae​(6)=be​(6)=te​(6)/2=4a_{e}(6)=b_{e}(6)=t_{e}(6)/2=4.

Theorem 4.

For every N≥1N\geq 1,

ae​(N)=be​(N)=te​(N)2.a_{e}(N)=b_{e}(N)=\frac{t_{e}(N)}{2}.

We now turn to strict odd-length partitions and OEIS A344650.

OEIS A344650 is the sequence whose nn-th term counts the number of strict partitions of 2​n2n into an odd number of parts; equivalently, it counts partitions of 2​n2n into an odd number of distinct parts [13]. We denote this sequence by a⁡(n)a(n) and write

A⁡(q):=∑n≥0a⁡(n)​qn.A(q):=\sum_{n\geq 0}a(n)q^{n}.

The comparison with To​(q)T_{o}(q) is given later in Remark 4.

For partitions into distinct parts, let pd​(k,n)p_{d}(k,n) denote the number of partitions of nn into exactly kk distinct positive parts.

Definition 2.

Define

podd​(n):=∑r≥0pd​(2​r+1,n),Podd​(q):=∑n≥0podd​(n)​qn.p_{\mathrm{odd}}(n):=\sum_{r\geq 0}p_{d}(2r+1,n),\qquad P_{\mathrm{odd}}(q):=\sum_{n\geq 0}p_{\mathrm{odd}}(n)q^{n}.

a⁡(n)=podd​(2​n)(n≥0).a(n)=p_{\mathrm{odd}}(2n)\qquad(n\geq 0). (3.2)

(8),(5,2,1),(4,3,1).(8),\qquad(5,2,1),\qquad(4,3,1).

We now make explicit the comparison between To​(q)T_{o}(q) and OEIS A344650. By Theorem 5,

(q,q)∞q​A​(q)=1+q5−q6+q11+q13+q14−q15+O⁡(q16).\frac{(q;q)_{\infty}}{q}A(q)=1+q^{5}-q^{6}+q^{11}+q^{13}+q^{14}-q^{15}+O(q^{16}).

4. Analytic formulas for the companion series

In this section we collect the analytic identities for the companion series and for the eta-normalized series

C⁡(q):=(q,q)∞​To​(q).C(q):=(q;q)_{\infty}T_{o}(q).

For convenience, write

Θ⁡(q)\displaystyle\Theta(q) :=∑r≥0(−1)r​qr⁡(r+1)/2,\displaystyle:=\sum_{r\geq 0}(-1)^{r}q^{r(r+1)/2}, (4.1)
Ψ⁡(q)\displaystyle\Psi(q) :=(q2,q2)∞(q,q2)∞.\displaystyle:=\frac{(q^{2};q^{2})_{\infty}}{(q;q^{2})_{\infty}}. (4.2)

Note that by Gauss’ sum (2.4) we have

Ψ⁡(q)=∑n≥0qn⁡(n+1)/2.\Psi(q)=\sum_{n\geq 0}q^{n(n+1)/2}. (4.3)
Proposition 1.

We have

S1​(q)\displaystyle S_{1}(q) =Ψ⁡(q)​Te​(q)+2​q​To​(q),\displaystyle=\Psi(q)T_{e}(q)+2qT_{o}(q), (4.4)
=Θ⁡(q)+4​q​To​(q),\displaystyle=\Theta(q)+4qT_{o}(q), (4.5)
Ψ⁡(q)​Te​(q)\displaystyle\Psi(q)T_{e}(q) =Θ⁡(q)+2​q​To​(q).\displaystyle=\Theta(q)+2qT_{o}(q). (4.6)

Define

P⁡(q):=∑n≥0qn⁡(3​n+1)/2​(1−q2​n+1).P(q):=\sum_{n\geq 0}q^{n(3n+1)/2}(1-q^{2n+1}).

The next proposition will be used in the proof of Theorem 4.

Proposition 2.

We have

Te​(q)=P⁡(q)(q,q)∞.T_{e}(q)=\frac{P(q)}{(q;q)_{\infty}}. (4.7)

Combining Proposition 1 with Proposition 2, we obtain

2​q​C​(q)=Ψ⁡(q)​P​(q)−(q,q)∞​Θ​(q).2qC(q)=\Psi(q)P(q)-(q;q)_{\infty}\Theta(q). (4.8)
Remark 5.

The first identity (4.4) is the direct even–odd decomposition of S1​(q)S_{1}(q). In conjunction with this decomposition, the remaining identities (4.5) and (4.6) can also be recovered from Andrews’ identity for vd​(q)v_{d}(q). Since S1​(q)=vd​(q)S_{1}(q)=v_{d}(q), [4, Theorem 1, (1.4)] gives

S1​(q)=−Θ⁡(q)+2​(−q,q)∞2​P​(q).S_{1}(q)=-\Theta(q)+2(-q;q)_{\infty}^{2}P(q). (4.9)

On the other hand, Proposition 2, Euler’s identity (2.2), and

(q,q)∞=(q,q2)∞​(q2,q2)∞(q;q)_{\infty}=(q;q^{2})_{\infty}(q^{2};q^{2})_{\infty}

give

The quadratic form x2+3​y2x^{2}+3y^{2} that appears in Theorem 3 is naturally attached to the theta series

Proof of Theorem 2.

By (6.1), the right-hand side is supported on positive exponents divisible by 55. Hence the coefficient of qnq^{n} on the left vanishes whenever n≢0(mod5)n\not\equiv 0\pmod{5}, which is equivalent to

Since pp is an odd prime different from 33, the congruence

9. Proof of Theorem 4

Proof of Theorem 4.

Since

Combining this identity with Proposition 2, we obtain

to appear, forbids the part 4​n+34n+3, and leaves all other parts unrestricted. Hence it counts partitions whose first missing part among the positive integers not congruent to 1(mod4)1\pmod{4} is exactly 4​n+34n+3. Summing over n≥0n\geq 0 gives

∑N≥1ae​(N)​qN=Te​(q)−12.\sum_{N\geq 1}a_{e}(N)q^{N}=\frac{T_{e}(q)-1}{2}.

comparison of coefficients yields

ae​(N)=te​(N)2(N≥1).a_{e}(N)=\frac{t_{e}(N)}{2}\qquad(N\geq 1).

For the overpartition interpretation, the discussion preceding Definition 1 shows that te​(N)t_{e}(N) counts overpartitions of NN whose largest part is even, only even parts may be overlined, and the odd parts are distinct. Toggling the overline on the first occurrence of the largest part is a free involution on this set, so exactly half of these overpartitions have nonoverlined largest part. Therefore

be​(N)=te​(N)2(N≥1).b_{e}(N)=\frac{t_{e}(N)}{2}\qquad(N\geq 1).

Combining the two identities, we obtain

ae​(N)=be​(N)=te​(N)2(N≥1),a_{e}(N)=b_{e}(N)=\frac{t_{e}(N)}{2}\qquad(N\geq 1),

which proves Theorem 4. ∎

10. Proof of Theorem 5

We begin with the standard staircase lemma.

Lemma 4.

For each fixed k≥1k\geq 1,

∑n≥0pd​(k,n)​qn=qk⁡(k+1)/2(q,q)k.\sum_{n\geq 0}p_{d}(k,n)q^{n}=\frac{q^{k(k+1)/2}}{(q;q)_{k}}.
Proof.

Write a partition into exactly kk distinct positive parts as

λ1>λ2>⋯>λk≥1.\lambda_{1}>\lambda_{2}>\cdots>\lambda_{k}\geq 1.

Remove the staircase (k,k−1,…,1)(k,k-1,\dots,1) by setting

μi=λi−(k−i+1)(1≤i≤k).\mu_{i}=\lambda_{i}-(k-i+1)\qquad(1\leq i\leq k).

Then

μ1≥μ2≥⋯≥μk≥0,\mu_{1}\geq\mu_{2}\geq\cdots\geq\mu_{k}\geq 0,

so μ\mu is an ordinary partition with at most kk parts. Conversely, adding the staircase back to any partition with at most kk parts gives a partition into exactly kk distinct parts. The staircase contributes k⁡(k+1)/2k(k+1)/2, and the generating function for partitions with at most kk parts is 1/(q,q)k1/(q;q)_{k}; see, for example, Andrews [1, Chapter 1]. ∎

which confirms (3.3).

11. Concluding remarks and open problems

We conclude with two combinatorial problems and two conjectures.

Problem 1.

Give a direct combinatorial proof of the identity ae​(N)=be​(N)a_{e}(N)=b_{e}(N) in Theorem 4; equivalently, construct a bijection between the ordinary partitions counted by ae​(N)a_{e}(N) and the overpartitions counted by be​(N)b_{e}(N).

Problem 2.

Find a combinatorial proof of Theorem 1.

Remark 7.

The coefficients of C⁡(q)C(q) are much sparser than those of To​(q)T_{o}(q), but they do not remain in {−2,−1,0,1,2}\{-2,-1,0,1,2\}. For example,

c⁡(9884)=3,c⁡(11956)=−3,c⁡(94836)=4,c⁡(310324)=−5.c(9884)=3,\qquad c(11956)=-3,\qquad c(94836)=4,\qquad c(310324)=-5.
Conjecture 1.
lim supn→∞c⁡(n)\displaystyle\limsup_{n\to\infty}c(n) =+∞,\displaystyle=+\infty, (11.1)
lim infn→∞c⁡(n)\displaystyle\liminf_{n\to\infty}c(n) =−∞.\displaystyle=-\infty. (11.2)

Write

To​(q)=∑n≥0to​(n)​qn.T_{o}(q)=\sum_{n\geq 0}t_{o}(n)q^{n}.

By Proposition 1,

4​to​(n)=s1​(n+1)−ε⁡(n+1),4t_{o}(n)=s_{1}(n+1)-\varepsilon(n+1),

where

ε⁡(m)={(−1)r,m=tr​ for some ​r≥0,0,otherwise.\varepsilon(m)=\begin{cases}(-1)^{r},&m=t_{r}\text{ for some }r\geq 0,\\ 0,&\text{otherwise.}\end{cases}

Thus, whenever n+1n+1 is not triangular,

to​(n)=s1​(n+1)4.t_{o}(n)=\frac{s_{1}(n+1)}{4}.

In particular, any 22-adic divisibility statement for s1​(m)s_{1}(m) on nontriangular indices transfers directly to to​(m−1)t_{o}(m-1).

Conjecture 2.

If 8​n+98n+9 has a prime divisor p≡5,7(mod8)p\equiv 5,7\pmod{8} to odd exponent, equivalently if 8​n+98n+9 is not represented by x2+2​y2x^{2}+2y^{2}, then

to​(n)≡0(mod2).t_{o}(n)\equiv 0\pmod{2}.
